title: Λυκάων
titleEn: The Choked River and Lycaon’s Plea — Iliad 21.1–96
part: The Choked River and Lycaon’s Plea (21.1–96)
source: Homer, The Iliad, Greek text of D. B. Monro and T. W. Allen, Homeri Opera, tomi I–II, 3rd ed. (Oxford Classical Texts; Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1920), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg001.perseus-grc2, sha256 ae8b617018c6e5af. Text as printed: the edition sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: Achilles drives half the Trojans toward the city and the rest into the Xanthus, where they crowd and swim like locusts before a fire and like fish before a dolphin. He leaves his spear on the bank, leaps in with his sword and kills until his hands tire, then picks out twelve young men alive to pay for Patroclus and has them bound and sent to the ships. Then he meets Lycaon, a son of Priam, whom he once captured in his father’s orchard and sold to Lemnos; Lycaon was ransomed and got home, and twelve days later a god puts him again in Achilles’ hands. Achilles marvels aloud that the dead seem to return, and Lycaon ducks under his spear and clings to his knees, pleading as a suppliant that he is not Hector’s brother by the same mother.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὅτε δὴ πόρον ἷξον ἐϋρρεῖος ποταμοῖο
Ξάνθου δινήεντος, ὃν ἀθάνατος τέκετο Ζεύς,
sentences.tr:
all’ hote dē poron hixon eÿrreios potamoio
Xanthou dinēentos, hon athanatos teketo Zeus,
sentences.l:
But when now the ford they reached of the fair-flowing river,
of eddying Xanthus, whom immortal Zeus begot,
sentences.i: But when they came to the ford of the fair-flowing river, eddying Xanthus, whom immortal Zeus begot,
sentences.n: No subject is named: ‘they’ are Achilles and the Trojans he is driving before him, as the last book left them. These two lines stand word for word at 14.433–434, where the wounded Hector was carried to the same river, and the English is taken over from there. ἷξον is a plural aorist of ἱκνέομαι ‘come to, reach’, without the augment. ἐϋρρεῖος ‘fair-flowing’ and δινήεις ‘eddying’ are epithets of the river, and Ξάνθου, in the genitive, says whose ford it is. Zeus is named as the river’s father, ἀθάνατος ‘immortal’.

sentences.t:
ἔνθα διατμήξας τοὺς μὲν πεδίον δὲ δίωκε
πρὸς πόλιν, ᾗ περ Ἀχαιοὶ ἀτυζόμενοι φοβέοντο
ἤματι τῷ προτέρῳ, ὅτε μαίνετο φαίδιμος Ἕκτωρ·
sentences.tr:
entha diatmēxas tous men pedion de diōke
pros polin, hēi per Achaioi atyzomenoi phobeonto
ēmati tōi proterōi, hote maineto phaidimos Hektōr·
sentences.i: There he cut them in two and drove some of them toward the city across the plain, by the way the Achaeans had fled, dazed with fear, the day before, when glorious Hector raged;
sentences.n: The subject is Achilles, still unnamed. διατμήξας, the aorist participle of διατμήγω, is ‘having cut apart’: he splits the fleeing army, and the other half is dealt with from line 7. τοὺς μέν ‘some of them’ waits for its answer there. πεδίον δέ has the suffix -δε of direction, ‘to the plain’. ᾗ περ is a relative of place or way, ‘by which, where’. ἀτυζόμενοι ‘dazed with fear’ and φοβέοντο ‘fled’ are said of the Achaeans: the poet sets the Trojans’ rout beside the Achaeans’ of the day before. φαίδιμος Ἕκτωρ ‘glorious Hector’ is Hector’s stock epithet.

sentences.t:
τῇ ῥ’ οἵ γε προχέοντο πεφυζότες, ἠέρα δ’ Ἥρη
πίτνα πρόσθε βαθεῖαν ἐρυκέμεν·
sentences.tr:
tēi rh’ hoi ge procheonto pephyzotes, ēera d’ Hērē
pitna prosthe batheian erykemen·
sentences.l:
that way they poured forth, put to flight, and a mist Hera
spread in front, deep, to hold them back;
sentences.i: That way they poured out in flight, and Hera spread a deep mist in front of them to hold them back;
sentences.n: τῇ ‘that way’ points to the road to the city, and οἵ γε ‘they’ are the Trojans Achilles drove that way. Hera spreads a mist to hold them up; the Greek gives ἐρυκέμεν no object, and since Hera favours the Achaeans, it is the fugitives she checks. ἐρυκέμεν is an epic infinitive in -έμεν, here of purpose. πίτνα is an imperfect of πίτνημι ‘spread’, without the augment, and πρόσθε ‘in front’. ἠέρα … βαθεῖαν ‘deep mist’ is split by the name Ἥρη, which stands between them. προχέοντο ‘poured forth’ is the verb for a crowd streaming out. πεφυζότες is a perfect participle of the rout-word φύζα, ‘in headlong flight’.

sentences.t:
ἡμίσεες δὲ
ἐς ποταμὸν εἰλεῦντο βαθύρροον ἀργυροδίνην,
ἐν δ’ ἔπεσον μεγάλῳ πατάγῳ, βράχε δ’ αἰπὰ ῥέεθρα,
ὄχθαι δ’ ἀμφὶ περὶ μεγάλ’ ἴαχον·
sentences.tr:
hēmisees de
es potamon eileunto bathyrroon argyrodinēn,
en d’ epeson megalōi patagōi, brache d’ aipa rheethra,
ochthai d’ amphi peri megal’ iachon·
sentences.l:
and half of them
into the river were crowded, deep-flowing, silver-eddying,
and fell in with a great crash, and the steep streams resounded,
and the banks round about loudly rang;
sentences.i: and half of them were crowded into the deep-flowing, silver-eddying river and fell in with a great crash, and the steep streams roared, and the banks rang loudly all around;
sentences.n: ἡμίσεες is the epic form of ‘halves’, so ‘half of them’, and it answers the τοὺς μέν of line 3. βαθύρροον ‘deep-flowing’ and ἀργυροδίνην ‘silver-eddying’ are the river’s fixed epithets, both in the accusative with ποταμόν. εἰλεῦντο is the imperfect passive of εἰλέω ‘press, crowd together’. πατάγῳ is a dative, ‘with a crash’. ῥέεθρα, the plural of ῥέεθρον, is the word for a stream or its bed, ‘the streams’. ἀμφὶ περί are two adverbs together, ‘all around’; μεγάλ’ is the neuter plural used as an adverb, ‘loudly’. ἴαχον is a past tense of ‘ring, cry out’.

sentences.t:
οἳ δ’ ἀλαλητῷ
ἔννεον ἔνθα καὶ ἔνθα ἑλισσόμενοι περὶ δίνας.
sentences.tr:
hoi d’ alalētōi
enneon entha kai entha helissomenoi peri dinas.
sentences.l:
and they with outcry
swam here and there, turning about the eddies.
sentences.i: and with a great outcry they swam this way and that, turning round the eddies.
sentences.n: οἳ δ’ ‘and they’: the article-form is a pronoun again. ἀλαλητῷ is a dative, ‘with outcry’: ἀλαλητός is the shouting of an army. ἔννεον is an imperfect of νέω ‘swim’. ἔνθα καὶ ἔνθα ‘here and there’ is a fixed phrase for aimless movement. ἑλισσόμενοι is a middle participle of ἑλίσσω ‘turn, wind’, and δίνας, the accusative of δίνη, is ‘eddies’: the same word is inside the epithets δινήεις and ἀργυροδίνης.

sentences.t:
ὡς δ’ ὅθ’ ὑπὸ ῥιπῆς πυρὸς ἀκρίδες ἠερέθονται
φευγέμεναι ποταμὸν δέ·
sentences.tr:
hōs d’ hoth’ hypo rhipēs pyros akrides ēerethontai
pheugemenai potamon de·
sentences.l:
And as when, before the rush of fire, locusts are fluttering
to flee toward a river;
sentences.i: And as when, before the rush of fire, locusts flutter up to flee toward a river,
sentences.n: A simile begins: ὡς δ’ ὅθ’ ‘and as when’. ἀκρίδες are locusts or grasshoppers. ὑπό with the genitive ῥιπῆς ‘rush’ means ‘driven by, away from’: the rush of the fire is what sets the locusts flying. ἠερέθονται ‘are fluttering’ is a verb for things that hover or move lightly in the air. φευγέμεναι is an epic infinitive of purpose, ‘to flee’, and ποταμὸν δέ again has the -δε of direction.

sentences.t:
τὸ δὲ φλέγει ἀκάματον πῦρ
ὄρμενον ἐξαίφνης, ταὶ δὲ πτώσσουσι καθ’ ὕδωρ·
sentences.tr:
to de phlegei akamaton pyr
ormenon exaiphnēs, tai de ptōssousi kath’ hydōr·
sentences.l:
and it blazes, the untiring fire,
starting up suddenly, and they cower down in the water;
sentences.i: while the untiring fire, starting up suddenly, blazes, and they cower down in the water;
sentences.n: τὸ δέ ‘and it’ is the fire; ἀκάματον πῦρ ‘untiring fire’ is a fixed phrase. ὄρμενον is a participle of ὄρνυμι in the middle, ‘rising, rushing up’. ταί is the feminine plural article-form used as a pronoun, ‘they’, meaning the locusts, which are feminine in Greek. πτώσσουσι ‘cower’ is the verb used for the Trojans at line 26: the simile’s locusts crouch in water as the men crouch under the banks.

sentences.t:
ὣς ὑπ’ Ἀχιλλῆος Ξάνθου βαθυδινήεντος
πλῆτο ῥόος κελάδων ἐπιμὶξ ἵππων τε καὶ ἀνδρῶν.
sentences.tr:
hōs hyp’ Achillēos Xanthou bathydinēentos
plēto rhoos keladōn epimix hippōn te kai andrōn.
sentences.l:
so before Achilles the roaring current of deep-eddying Xanthus
was filled with horses and men, in confusion.
sentences.i: so before Achilles the roaring current of deep-eddying Xanthus was filled with horses and men in confusion.
sentences.n: ὣς ‘so’ closes the simile and brings it back to the river. ὑπ’ Ἀχιλλῆος is ὑπό with the genitive, ‘under the pressure of Achilles’. πλῆτο is an unaugmented aorist passive of πίμπλημι, and ‘filled’ takes the genitive: ἵππων τε καὶ ἀνδρῶν ‘with horses and men’. ῥόος is the epic form of ῥοῦς ‘current’, and κελάδων ‘roaring’ is a participle. ἐπιμίξ ‘in confusion’ is a rare adverb. βαθυδινήεντος ‘deep-eddying’ matches βαθύρροον in line 8.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ὃ διογενὴς δόρυ μὲν λίπεν αὐτοῦ ἐπ’ ὄχθῃ
κεκλιμένον μυρίκῃσιν, ὃ δ’ ἔσθορε δαίμονι ἶσος
φάσγανον οἶον ἔχων, κακὰ δὲ φρεσὶ μήδετο ἔργα,
τύπτε δ’ ἐπιστροφάδην·
sentences.tr:
autar ho diogenēs dory men lipen autou ep’ ochthēi
keklimenon myrikēisin, ho d’ esthore daimoni isos
phasganon oion echōn, kaka de phresi mēdeto erga,
typte d’ epistrophadēn·
sentences.l:
But he, Zeus-sprung, the spear indeed left there on the bank,
leaning against the tamarisks, and he leapt in, equal to a divinity,
holding only his sword, and evil deeds in his wits devised,
and struck, turning from one to another;
sentences.i: But he, the Zeus-born, left his spear there on the bank, leaning against the tamarisks, and leapt in, like a divinity, holding only his sword, and devising evil deeds in his wits, and struck, wheeling from one man to the next;
sentences.n: The edition begins a new paragraph; Achilles is the subject, ὃ διογενής ‘he, the Zeus-born’, and διογενής is applied to heroes in general. He leaves his spear on the bank (δόρυ μέν … ὃ δ’ ‘the spear on the one hand, but he …’) and leaps into the river with only the sword (φάσγανον οἶον ἔχων ‘holding the sword alone’). μυρίκῃσιν is a dative plural, the tamarisks, a shrub of river banks. ἔσθορε is a past tense of ἐσθρῴσκω ‘leap in’, without the augment. δαίμονι ἶσος ‘like a divinity’ compares him to a power greater than a man. κακὰ … ἔργα μήδετο: ‘he was devising evil deeds’, with φρεσί ‘in his wits’. ἐπιστροφάδην is an adverb, ‘turning from one to another’. Line 18 is metrically irregular as the scansion table reads it, at μυρίκῃσιν: the υ, which the table counts long, has to be read short.

sentences.t:
τῶν δὲ στόνος ὄρνυτ’ ἀεικὴς
ἄορι θεινομένων, ἐρυθαίνετο δ’ αἵματι ὕδωρ.
sentences.tr:
tōn de stonos ornyt’ aeikēs
aori theinomenōn, erythaineto d’ haimati hydōr.
sentences.l:
and of them a groaning arose, unseemly,
as they were struck with the sword, and was reddened with blood the water.
sentences.i: and an unseemly groaning rose from them as they were struck with the sword, and the water was reddened with blood.
sentences.n: τῶν δέ ‘and of them’ with στόνος ‘groaning’ means the groaning that comes from the struck men; ἀεικής ‘unseemly’ is the adjective for sounds and sights that should not be. ἄορι θεινομένων is a genitive absolute: ἄορ is a second word for ‘sword’, and θεινομένων ‘being struck’ is a passive participle. ὄρνυτ’ is ὄρνυτο, the imperfect middle of ὄρνυμι ‘rise’, and ἐρυθαίνετο ‘was reddened’ is an imperfect passive.

sentences.t:
ὡς δ’ ὑπὸ δελφῖνος μεγακήτεος ἰχθύες ἄλλοι
φεύγοντες πιμπλᾶσι μυχοὺς λιμένος εὐόρμου
δειδιότες· μάλα γάρ τε κατεσθίει ὅν κε λάβῃσιν·
sentences.tr:
hōs d’ hypo delphinos megakēteos ichthyes alloi
pheugontes pimplasi mychous limenos euormou
deidiotes· mala gar te katesthiei hon ke labēisin·
sentences.i: And as the other fish flee before a huge dolphin and fill the inner nooks of a harbour with good anchorage, in fear, for it devours whichever one it catches;
sentences.n: A second simile, this time of fish; line 25 applies it at once. ὑπὸ δελφῖνος ‘from before a dolphin’: ὑπό with the genitive again gives the cause of flight. μεγακήτεος ‘huge’ is probably μέγα- + κῆτος ‘sea-monster’, but the formation is not secure. ἰχθύες ἄλλοι ‘other fish’ counts the dolphin among the fish. πιμπλᾶσι is a form of πίμπλημι ‘fill’; μυχούς ‘inner nooks’; εὐόρμου ‘with good anchorage’. δειδιότες is a perfect participle of δείδω ‘fear’. In μάλα γάρ τε the τε marks a general truth, and ὅν κε λάβῃσιν, with κε and the subjunctive, is a general relative clause, ‘whichever it may catch’.

sentences.t:
ὣς Τρῶες ποταμοῖο κατὰ δεινοῖο ῥέεθρα
πτῶσσον ὑπὸ κρημνούς.
sentences.tr:
hōs Trōes potamoio kata deinoio rheethra
ptōsson hypo krēmnous.
sentences.l:
so the Trojans, along the streams of the dread river,
cowered under the steep banks.
sentences.i: so the Trojans cowered under the steep banks along the streams of the dread river.
sentences.n: ὣς Τρῶες applies the simile at once: the Trojans are the fish. κατὰ … ῥέεθρα is κατά with the accusative, ‘along, down’, and ποταμοῖο δεινοῖο is the epic genitive in -οιο, ‘of the dread river’. πτῶσσον ‘cowered’ is the imperfect of πτώσσω, which the locusts of line 14 also did. κρημνούς are the steep or overhanging banks. The unit ends in the middle of line 26, at a full stop.

sentences.t:
ὃ δ’ ἐπεὶ κάμε χεῖρας ἐναίρων,
ζωοὺς ἐκ ποταμοῖο δυώδεκα λέξατο κούρους
ποινὴν Πατρόκλοιο Μενοιτιάδαο θανόντος·
sentences.tr:
ho d’ epei kame cheiras enairōn,
zōous ek potamoio dyōdeka lexato kourous
poinēn Patrokloio Menoitiadao thanontos·
sentences.i: And when he had tired his hands with slaying, he picked out twelve youths alive from the river, as requital for Patroclus, the son of Menoetius, who was dead;
sentences.n: The unit begins in the middle of line 26. κάμε χεῖρας is ‘grew weary in his hands’, the accusative saying where the weariness is (an accusative of respect), and ἐναίρων is ‘slaying’. ζωούς ‘alive’ matters: these twelve are taken prisoner, not killed. λέξατο is an aorist middle of λέγω ‘pick out’. ποινήν ‘requital’ is what is owed for a killing; the Greek does not yet say what will be done with the twelve. Μενοιτιάδαο is a patronymic in the epic genitive -αο, and θανόντος is the aorist participle of θνῄσκω, ‘who had died’.

sentences.t:
τοὺς ἐξῆγε θύραζε τεθηπότας ἠΰτε νεβρούς,
δῆσε δ’ ὀπίσσω χεῖρας ἐϋτμήτοισιν ἱμᾶσι,
τοὺς αὐτοὶ φορέεσκον ἐπὶ στρεπτοῖσι χιτῶσι,
δῶκε δ’ ἑταίροισιν κατάγειν κοίλας ἐπὶ νῆας.
sentences.tr:
tous exēge thyraze tethēpotas ēÿte nebrous,
dēse d’ opissō cheiras eÿtmētoisin himasi,
tous autoi phoreeskon epi streptoisi chitōsi,
dōke d’ hetairoisin katagein koilas epi nēas.
sentences.l:
them he led outside, stunned like fawns,
and bound behind their hands with well-cut straps,
which they themselves used to wear on their twisted tunics,
and gave them to his companions to lead down to the hollow ships.
sentences.i: He led them out, stunned like fawns, and bound their hands behind them with well-cut straps, the straps they themselves used to wear over their twisted tunics, and gave them to his companions to take down to the hollow ships.
sentences.n: θύραζε ‘outside, out’ is built with the suffix -ζε of direction (compare -δε); τεθηπότας is a perfect participle ‘stunned’, ἠΰτε ‘like’, and νεβρούς ‘fawns’, a frightened-animal comparison. ὀπίσσω is ‘behind’ (their backs), and ἐϋτμήτοισιν ἱμᾶσι is a dative of means, ‘with well-cut straps’. τοὺς … φορέεσκον: τοὺς is a relative, ‘which’, referring to the straps, and the ending -εσκ- makes φορέεσκον an iterative, ‘used to wear’. στρεπτοῖσι χιτῶσι is literally ‘twisted tunics’; what sort of tunic is meant is not known. κατάγειν is ‘to bring down’, to the ships on the shore.

sentences.t: αὐτὰρ ὃ ἂψ ἐπόρουσε δαϊζέμεναι μενεαίνων.
sentences.tr: autar ho aps eporouse daïzemenai meneainōn.
sentences.l: But he again rushed on to rend, eager.
sentences.i: But he sprang to the attack again, eager to rend them.
sentences.n: ἂψ ἐπόρουσε ‘rushed on again’: ἂψ is ‘back, again’, and ἐπόρουσε is the aorist of ἐπορούω ‘rush upon’, here a return to the killing. δαϊζέμεναι is an epic infinitive in -έμεναι of δαΐζω ‘rend’, and μενεαίνων ‘eager’ is a participle. The line shuts the picture of the carnage and turns to a single man.

sentences.t:
ἔνθ’ υἷι Πριάμοιο συνήντετο Δαρδανίδαο
ἐκ ποταμοῦ φεύγοντι Λυκάονι, τόν ῥά ποτ’ αὐτὸς
ἦγε λαβὼν ἐκ πατρὸς ἀλωῆς οὐκ ἐθέλοντα
ἐννύχιος προμολών·
sentences.tr:
enth’ huii Priamoio synēnteto Dardanidao
ek potamou pheugonti Lykaoni, ton rha pot’ autos
ēge labōn ek patros alōēs ouk ethelonta
ennychios promolōn·
sentences.l:
Then upon the son of Priam the Dardanid he came face to face,
fleeing from the river, Lycaon, whom once he himself
had led away, taking him from his father’s orchard, unwilling,
coming forth by night;
sentences.i: Then he met the son of Priam the Dardanid, Lycaon, as he fled from the river, the man whom Achilles himself had once taken from his father’s orchard against his will, coming forth by night;
sentences.n: The edition begins a new paragraph, and a new person: Lycaon, whose name does not come until the second line, in the dative with φεύγοντι. συνήντετο takes the dative, ‘met’. Δαρδανίδαο is a patronymic from Dardanus, the ancestor of the royal house of Troy, in the epic genitive -αο, so ‘Priam the Dardanid’. τόν ῥά ποτ’ αὐτὸς ἦγε λαβών opens a backward look: ‘whom once he himself took and led away’, and the story runs to line 48. ἀλωῆς is a planted ground, an orchard, for the word is also used of a threshing-floor. ἐννύχιος is ‘by night’, and προμολών ‘coming forth’. The unit ends in the middle of line 37.

sentences.t:
ὃ δ’ ἐρινεὸν ὀξέϊ χαλκῷ
τάμνε νέους ὄρπηκας, ἵν’ ἅρματος ἄντυγες εἶεν·
sentences.tr:
ho d’ erineon oxeï chalkōi
tamne neous orpēkas, hin’ harmatos antyges eien·
sentences.l:
and he a wild fig-tree with sharp bronze
was cutting, young shoots, that of a chariot rails might be;
sentences.i: and he was cutting young shoots from a wild fig-tree with sharp bronze, to be rails for a chariot;
sentences.n: The unit begins in the middle of line 37. ὃ δέ ‘and he’ is Lycaon, who was at work in the orchard. ἐρινεόν is the wild fig-tree, and ὄρπηκας νέους ‘young shoots’ stands beside it as a second accusative: he cut the tree for its shoots. ὀξέϊ χαλκῷ is ‘with sharp bronze’, a blade. ἵν’ … εἶεν is a purpose clause with the optative, ‘so that they might be’, and ἄντυγες are the curved rails of a chariot.

sentences.t: τῷ δ’ ἄρ’ ἀνώϊστον κακὸν ἤλυθε δῖος Ἀχιλλεύς.
sentences.tr: tōi d’ ar’ anōïston kakon ēlythe dios Achilleus.
sentences.l: and upon him, then, an unlooked-for evil came, heavenly Achilles.
sentences.i: But upon him an unforeseen evil came: heavenly Achilles.
sentences.n: τῷ δ’ ἄρ’ ‘and upon him, then’: the dative says whom the evil came to. ἀνώϊστον, ‘unforeseen’, is a negative form of the stem of οἴομαι ‘expect’, and κακόν ‘evil’ is said of Achilles himself, who stands in the last words of the line, δῖος Ἀχιλλεύς ‘heavenly Achilles’, in apposition. ἤλυθε is an epic form of ἦλθε.

sentences.t:
καὶ τότε μέν μιν Λῆμνον ἐϋκτιμένην ἐπέρασσε
νηυσὶν ἄγων, ἀτὰρ υἱὸς Ἰήσονος ὦνον ἔδωκε·
sentences.tr:
kai tote men min Lēmnon eÿktimenēn eperasse
nēusin agōn, atar huios Iēsonos ōnon edōke·
sentences.l:
And then, for that time, him to well-built Lemnos he sold,
leading him in ships; and the son of Jason gave the price;
sentences.i: That time he took him in ships to well-settled Lemnos and sold him, and the son of Jason paid the price;
sentences.n: καὶ τότε μέν ‘and for that time’: the μέν waits for the next lines, which tell what came after. μιν is Lycaon. ἐπέρασσε is a past tense of περάω ‘carry across and sell’, and ἄγων ‘leading, taking him’. ἐϋκτιμένην ‘well-built’ in the literal layer is the epithet of towns and islands, and the free layer says ‘well-settled’. Ἰήσονος is the genitive of Jason, and ὦνον is ‘the price’ paid for a purchase.

sentences.t:
κεῖθεν δὲ ξεῖνός μιν ἐλύσατο πολλὰ δ’ ἔδωκεν
Ἴμβριος Ἠετίων, πέμψεν δ’ ἐς δῖαν Ἀρίσβην·
sentences.tr:
keithen de xeinos min elysato polla d’ edōken
Imbrios Ēetiōn, pempsen d’ es dian Arisbēn·
sentences.l:
and from there a guest-friend ransomed him, and much gave
the Imbrian Eetion, and sent him to heavenly Arisbe;
sentences.i: and from there a guest-friend, Eetion of Imbros, ransomed him, giving much, and sent him to heavenly Arisbe;
sentences.n: ξεῖνος is a guest-friend, a man tied to another by the bond of hospitality, and the name comes after the verb: Ἠετίων. Ἴμβριος is an adjective, ‘of Imbros’, the island. ἐλύσατο is an aorist middle of λύω in the sense ‘ransom’, and πολλὰ … ἔδωκεν ‘gave much’ says what he paid. πέμψεν is an unaugmented aorist ‘sent’. δῖαν ‘heavenly’ is the usual epithet for places as well as men. Arisbe is a town in the Troad.

sentences.t: ἔνθεν ὑπεκπροφυγὼν πατρώϊον ἵκετο δῶμα.
sentences.tr: enthen hypekprophygōn patrōïon hiketo dōma.
sentences.l: From there, having slipped away, he came to his father’s house.
sentences.i: From there he slipped away and came to his father’s house.
sentences.n: ἔνθεν ‘from there’ has the suffix -θεν of ‘from’. ὑπεκπροφυγών is a participle built from φεύγω with three prefixes (ὑπό, ἐκ, πρό): ‘having slipped away out and forth’. ἵκετο is an unaugmented aorist ‘came’. πατρώϊον is the adjective ‘of his father’, here ‘his father’s house’.

sentences.t:
ἕνδεκα δ’ ἤματα θυμὸν ἐτέρπετο οἷσι φίλοισιν
ἐλθὼν ἐκ Λήμνοιο·
sentences.tr:
hendeka d’ ēmata thymon eterpeto hoisi philoisin
elthōn ek Lēmnoio·
sentences.l:
For eleven days his heart he delighted with his own dear ones,
having come from Lemnos;
sentences.i: For eleven days, back from Lemnos, he delighted his heart among his own dear ones;
sentences.n: ἕνδεκα δ’ ἤματα ‘for eleven days’: an accusative of duration. θυμὸν ἐτέρπετο is ‘he delighted his heart’ (a middle verb with its object in the accusative). οἷσι is the possessive ὅς in the dative plural, ‘his own’, easily mistaken for the relative, and φίλοισιν ‘dear ones’ means family and friends. ἐλθὼν ἐκ Λήμνοιο has the epic genitive in -οιο. The unit ends in the middle of line 46.

sentences.t:
δυωδεκάτῃ δέ μιν αὖτις
χερσὶν Ἀχιλλῆος θεὸς ἔμβαλεν, ὅς μιν ἔμελλε
πέμψειν εἰς Ἀΐδαο καὶ οὐκ ἐθέλοντα νέεσθαι.
sentences.tr:
dyōdekatēi de min autis
chersin Achillēos theos embalen, hos min emelle
pempsein eis Aïdao kai ouk ethelonta neesthai.
sentences.l:
and on the twelfth, him again
into the hands of Achilles a god threw, who was destined him
to send to Hades’, though unwilling to go.
sentences.i: and on the twelfth day a god threw him again into the hands of Achilles, who was to send him to the house of Hades, though he did not want to go.
sentences.n: The unit begins in the middle of line 46. δυωδεκάτῃ is the dative of time, ‘on the twelfth’ (day understood). θεὸς ἔμβαλεν, ‘a god threw him in’, is how the poet marks fate: no god is named. ὅς takes the nearer word, Ἀχιλλῆος, as its antecedent, and ἔμελλε with the infinitive is ‘was destined to’. Ἀΐδαο is the epic genitive of Hades, and ‘the house’ is understood. νέεσθαι is an epic infinitive ‘to go’. Lycaon will count the same twelve days himself at line 81.

sentences.t:
τὸν δ’ ὡς οὖν ἐνόησε ποδάρκης δῖος Ἀχιλλεὺς
γυμνὸν ἄτερ κόρυθός τε καὶ ἀσπίδος, οὐδ’ ἔχεν ἔγχος,
ἀλλὰ τὰ μέν ῥ’ ἀπὸ πάντα χαμαὶ βάλε·
sentences.tr:
ton d’ hōs oun enoēse podarkēs dios Achilleus
gymnon ater korythos te kai aspidos, oud’ echen enchos,
alla ta men rh’ apo panta chamai bale·
sentences.i: And when swift-footed, heavenly Achilles noticed him, naked, without helmet or shield, holding no spear, but with all those things thrown down on the ground,
sentences.n: The sentence is the standing opening τὸν δ’ ὡς οὖν ἐνόησε ‘and when he noticed him’, with the name and epithet filling the second half of the line; its main verb, εἶπε, does not come until line 53. ποδάρκης ‘swift-footed’ is Achilles’ epithet here (the formation is uncertain, probably πούς + ἀρκέω), and δῖος ‘heavenly’. γυμνόν ‘naked’ means stripped of armour, not of clothes: ἄτερ + the genitive is ‘without’. βάλε is an aorist in the sense of a pluperfect, ‘had thrown’, and τὰ … πάντα ‘all those things’ are the helmet, shield and spear just named. The unit ends in the middle of line 51.

sentences.t:
τεῖρε γὰρ ἱδρὼς
φεύγοντ’ ἐκ ποταμοῦ, κάματος δ’ ὑπὸ γούνατ’ ἐδάμνα·
sentences.tr:
teire gar hidrōs
pheugont’ ek potamou, kamatos d’ hypo gounat’ edamna·
sentences.l:
for sweat wore him down
as he fled from the river, and weariness beneath was subduing his knees;
sentences.i: for sweat was wearing him down as he fled from the river, and weariness was overcoming his knees;
sentences.n: The unit begins in the middle of line 51 and gives the reason Lycaon threw his arms down. τεῖρε is the imperfect of τείρω ‘wear out’, and its object is not named: ‘him’. φεύγοντ’ is a participle in the accusative, agreeing with that ‘him’. ὑπὸ … ἐδάμνα is a tmesis, the preverb ὑπό standing apart from the verb, ‘was subduing from beneath’; ἐδάμνα is an imperfect of δάμνημι ‘subdue’, and γούνατ’ is the elided plural γούνατα ‘knees’.

sentences.t: ὀχθήσας δ’ ἄρα εἶπε πρὸς ὃν μεγαλήτορα θυμόν·
sentences.tr: ochthēsas d’ ara eipe pros hon megalētora thymon·
sentences.l: And, vexed, he then spoke to his own great-spirited heart:
sentences.i: And, troubled, he spoke to his own great-spirited heart:
sentences.n: The line announces a speech to himself. ὀχθήσας is an aorist participle ‘vexed, troubled’, εἶπε ‘spoke’, and ὃν … θυμόν is the possessive ὅς, ‘his own heart’. μεγαλήτορα ‘great-spirited’ is an epithet kept in the same words each time. The line is word for word 11.403, where Odysseus speaks to himself, and it is also found at Odyssey 5.298 and 5.355.

sentences.t: ὢ πόποι ἦ μέγα θαῦμα τόδ’ ὀφθαλμοῖσιν ὁρῶμαι·
sentences.tr: ō popoi ē mega thauma tod’ ophthalmoisin horōmai·
sentences.l: “Ah, truly a great wonder this with my eyes I behold:
sentences.i: “Ah, this is truly a great wonder that I behold with my own eyes:
sentences.n: ὢ πόποι is a cry of surprise, ‘Ah’; ἦ is ‘truly’; μέγα θαῦμα τόδ’ is ‘this great wonder’. ὀφθαλμοῖσιν is a dative of means with ὁρῶμαι ‘I behold’, a verb with a passive-looking ending but an active sense. The wonder is announced first and explained next. The first half of this line is also Poseidon’s at 13.99, where a different line follows.

sentences.t:
ἦ μάλα δὴ Τρῶες μεγαλήτορες οὕς περ ἔπεφνον
αὖτις ἀναστήσονται ὑπὸ ζόφου ἠερόεντος,
οἷον δὴ καὶ ὅδ’ ἦλθε φυγὼν ὕπο νηλεὲς ἦμαρ
Λῆμνον ἐς ἠγαθέην πεπερημένος·
sentences.tr:
ē mala dē Trōes megalētores hous per epephnon
autis anastēsontai hypo zophou ēeroentos,
hoion dē kai hod’ ēlthe phygōn hypo nēlees ēmar
Lēmnon es ēgatheēn peperēmenos·
sentences.l:
Truly now the great-spirited Trojans, even those whom I killed,
will rise again from beneath the misty gloom,
seeing how this one too has come, having fled the pitiless day,
to holy Lemnos, sold across;
sentences.i: Surely the great-spirited Trojans whom I have killed will rise again from the misty gloom — see how this man too has come back, having escaped the pitiless day, sold off to holy Lemnos;
sentences.n: He is looking at Lycaon and finds in him the proof that the dead may return: sold abroad, and here again. ἦ μάλα δή is ‘truly indeed’, and οὕς περ ἔπεφνον ‘even those whom I killed’ uses ἔπεφνον, an aorist ‘killed’. ἀναστήσονται is a future ‘will rise up’, and ὑπὸ ζόφου ἠερόεντος ‘from under the misty gloom’ is the underworld. οἷον δή is an exclamation, ‘see how’. φυγὼν ὕπο νηλεὲς ἦμαρ is a tmesis, ὕπο standing apart from the participle it belongs to (ὑποφυγών), ‘escaping the pitiless day’, the day of death. πεπερημένος is a perfect passive participle of περάω ‘sell abroad’, which picks up ἐπέρασσε at line 40, and ἠγαθέην ‘holy’ is the epithet of Lemnos. The unit ends in the middle of line 58.

sentences.t:
οὐδέ μιν ἔσχε
πόντος ἁλὸς πολιῆς, ὃ πολέας ἀέκοντας ἐρύκει.
sentences.tr:
oude min esche
pontos halos poliēs, ho poleas aekontas erykei.
sentences.l:
and him did not hold
the deep of the grey sea, which many unwilling holds back.
sentences.i: and the deep of the grey sea, which holds many back against their will, did not hold him.
sentences.n: The unit begins in the middle of line 58. οὐδέ μιν ἔσχε ‘nor did it hold him’: ἔσχε is an aorist ‘held, kept back’, and the sea normally does hold men back from returning. πόντος ἁλὸς πολιῆς ‘the deep of the grey sea’, with πολιῆς, the genitive ‘grey’, agreeing with ἁλός. πολέας is the epic accusative plural of πολύς, ‘many’, and ἀέκοντας is ‘unwilling’, men who would go home if the sea let them. ὃ is the relative ‘which’, the sea.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἄγε δὴ καὶ δουρὸς ἀκωκῆς ἡμετέροιο
γεύσεται, ὄφρα ἴδωμαι ἐνὶ φρεσὶν ἠδὲ δαείω
ἢ ἄρ’ ὁμῶς καὶ κεῖθεν ἐλεύσεται, ἦ μιν ἐρύξει
γῆ φυσίζοος, ἥ τε κατὰ κρατερόν περ ἐρύκει.
sentences.tr:
all’ age dē kai douros akōkēs hēmeteroio
geusetai, ophra idōmai eni phresin ēde daeiō
ē ar’ homōs kai keithen eleusetai, ē min eryxei
gē physizoos, hē te kata krateron per erykei.
sentences.l:
But come now, also of the spear’s tip, ours,
he shall taste, that I may see in my wits and learn
whether likewise even from there he will come, or him will hold
the life-giving earth, which holds down even the strong.”
sentences.i: But come now, he shall taste the tip of my spear as well, so that I may see and learn in my wits whether he will come back from there likewise, or the life-giving earth will hold him, which holds down even the strong.”
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ἄγε δή, ‘but come now’, followed by a future (γεύσεται ‘he shall taste’), is a resolution Achilles makes to himself; γεύσεται takes the genitive δουρὸς ἀκωκῆς, ‘the tip of the spear’. ἡμετέροιο ‘our’ stands for ‘my’. ἴδωμαι and δαείω are subjunctives of purpose, ‘that I may see’ and ‘that I may learn’, and ἢ … ἦ is ‘whether … or’. κεῖθεν ‘from there’ is the world below, and ὁμῶς καὶ ‘likewise even’. φυσίζοος ‘life-giving’ is the epithet of the earth, and κατὰ … ἐρύκει is a tmesis, ‘holds down’. The speech ends here; the test he proposes is to kill Lycaon and see whether the earth keeps him.

sentences.t: ὣς ὅρμαινε μένων·
sentences.tr: hōs hormaine menōn·
sentences.l: So he pondered, waiting;
sentences.i: So he pondered, standing there;
sentences.n: The edition begins a new paragraph. ὣς ‘so’ closes the speech and ὅρμαινε ‘was pondering’ is the imperfect of ὁρμαίνω, the verb of a hero weighing what to do. μένων is ‘waiting, standing his ground’. The unit ends in the middle of line 64, at the ano teleia.

sentences.t:
ὃ δέ οἱ σχεδὸν ἦλθε τεθηπὼς
γούνων ἅψασθαι μεμαώς, περὶ δ’ ἤθελε θυμῷ
ἐκφυγέειν θάνατόν τε κακὸν καὶ κῆρα μέλαιναν.
sentences.tr:
ho de hoi schedon ēlthe tethēpōs
gounōn hapsasthai memaōs, peri d’ ēthele thymōi
ekphygeein thanaton te kakon kai kēra melainan.
sentences.l:
and he came near him, stunned,
eager to touch his knees, and exceedingly in his heart he wished
to escape evil death and the black death-fate.
sentences.i: and the other came up close to him, stunned, eager to touch his knees, and with all his heart he wished to escape evil death and the black spirit of death.
sentences.n: The unit begins in the middle of line 64. ὃ δέ ‘and he’ is Lycaon, the other man. οἱ is the dative ‘to him’ and σχεδόν ‘near’. τεθηπώς ‘stunned’ is the participle of line 29, and μεμαώς ‘eager’ is a perfect participle. γούνων ἅψασθαι ‘to touch his knees’ takes the genitive, the suppliant’s gesture. περὶ δ’ ἤθελε θυμῷ: περί here is an adverb, ‘exceedingly’, and θυμῷ ‘in his heart’. ἐκφυγέειν is an epic infinitive. κῆρα μέλαιναν is ‘the black death-fate’: κήρ, ‘death-spirit’, is a different word from κῆρ ‘heart’.

sentences.t:
ἤτοι ὃ μὲν δόρυ μακρὸν ἀνέσχετο δῖος Ἀχιλλεὺς
οὐτάμεναι μεμαώς, ὃ δ’ ὑπέδραμε καὶ λάβε γούνων
κύψας·
sentences.tr:
ētoi ho men dory makron anescheto dios Achilleus
outamenai memaōs, ho d’ hypedrame kai labe gounōn
kypsas·
sentences.i: For his part, heavenly Achilles held up his long spear, eager to wound him, and the other ran in under it and took hold of his knees, stooping;
sentences.n: ἤτοι is printed as one word in this edition. ὃ μέν … ὃ δ’ ‘the one … the other’ sets the two men side by side. ἀνέσχετο is an aorist middle of ἀνέχω, ‘held up’, and οὐτάμεναι is an epic infinitive of οὐτάω ‘wound, stab’, ‘to wound’. μεμαώς ‘eager’ is again the perfect participle. ὑπέδραμε is an aorist of ὑποτρέχω ‘run in under’, and λάβε γούνων ‘took hold of the knees’ takes the genitive. κύψας ‘stooping’ is how he ducks under the spear. The unit ends at the beginning of line 69.

sentences.t:
ἐγχείη δ’ ἄρ’ ὑπὲρ νώτου ἐνὶ γαίῃ
ἔστη ἱεμένη χροὸς ἄμεναι ἀνδρομέοιο.
sentences.tr:
encheiē d’ ar’ hyper nōtou eni gaiēi
estē hiemenē chroos amenai andromeoio.
sentences.l:
And the spear over his back into the earth
stood fast, eager to be sated on the flesh, a man’s.
sentences.i: and the spear went over his back and stood fast in the earth, eager to glut itself on human flesh.
sentences.n: The unit begins after the first word of line 69. ἐγχείη is one of the poet’s words for ‘spear’, as ἔγχος is in lines 50 and 72. ὑπὲρ νώτου ‘over his back’ says it flew over the stooping man, and ἔστη ‘stood’ means it stuck upright in the ground. ἱεμένη ‘eager’ and ἄμεναι ‘to be sated’, an infinitive of ἄω, personify the spear, which wants to feed on χροός ‘flesh’ (genitive). ἀνδρομέοιο is the adjective ‘of a man, human’ in the epic genitive -οιο.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ὃ τῇ ἑτέρῃ μὲν ἑλὼν ἐλλίσσετο γούνων,
τῇ δ’ ἑτέρῃ ἔχεν ἔγχος ἀκαχμένον οὐδὲ μεθίει·
sentences.tr:
autar ho tēi heterēi men helōn ellisseto gounōn,
tēi d’ heterēi echen enchos akachmenon oude methiei·
sentences.l:
But he, with the one hand, having taken hold of the knees, entreated,
and with the other held the pointed spear and did not let go;
sentences.i: With one hand he held Achilles’ knees and entreated him, and with the other he gripped the pointed spear and did not let it go;
sentences.n: The two hands are set against each other: τῇ ἑτέρῃ μέν … τῇ δ’ ἑτέρῃ ‘with the one … with the other’ (datives of means). γούνων most naturally goes with ἑλών, as with λάβε γούνων three lines earlier (line 68); ἑλών is ‘having taken hold’ and ἐλλίσσετο ‘entreated’. The spear in the other hand is presumably the one that stuck in the ground, and ἀκαχμένον ‘pointed’ is a perfect participle. οὐδὲ μεθίει is ‘and did not let go’.

sentences.t: καί μιν φωνήσας ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα·
sentences.tr: kai min phōnēsas epea pteroenta prosēuda·
sentences.l: and, lifting his voice, to him winged words he spoke:
sentences.i: and lifting his voice he spoke winged words to him:
sentences.n: φωνήσας is an aorist participle, ‘lifting his voice’, and ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα ‘he spoke winged words’ introduces a speech by a standing formula. μιν is masculine here, Achilles, so the English says ‘to him’; the same line stands at 1.201, where μιν was Athena. The line is also a formula in the Odyssey.

sentences.t: γουνοῦμαι σ’ Ἀχιλεῦ· σὺ δέ μ’ αἴδεο καί μ’ ἐλέησον·
sentences.tr: gounoumai s’ Achileu· sy de m’ aideo kai m’ eleēson·
sentences.l: “I beseech you at your knees, Achilles; and you, revere me, and pity me;
sentences.i: “I entreat you, Achilles; and you, show me respect and take pity on me;
sentences.n: Lycaon opens with the formal words of a suppliant: γουνοῦμαι is a verb made from γόνυ ‘knee’, ‘I beseech at the knees’. σ’ is σε, and Ἀχιλεῦ is the vocative, with the single λ of the metre. αἴδεο is the imperative of αἰδέομαι, ‘respect, revere’, in the uncontracted epic form, and ἐλέησον is an aorist imperative of ἐλεέω ‘pity’. The same line, with Odysseus for Achilles, opens a plea twice in the Odyssey (22.312 and 22.344).

sentences.t: ἀντί τοί εἰμ’ ἱκέταο διοτρεφὲς αἰδοίοιο·
sentences.tr: anti toi eim’ hiketao diotrephes aidoioio·
sentences.l: In place of a revered suppliant I am to you, Zeus-nurtured one;
sentences.i: I am to you as a revered suppliant, Zeus-nurtured one;
sentences.n: ἀντί with the genitive means ‘in place of, equal to’, so Lycaon asks to be treated as what he is, a suppliant. τοί here is τοι, the enclitic form of σοί ‘to you’, and not the particle. ἱκέταο is the epic genitive in -αο of ἱκέτης ‘suppliant’, and αἰδοίοιο, in -οιο, is ‘to be revered’. διοτρεφές is the vocative of διοτρεφής, ‘Zeus-nurtured’, an honorific that the poems give to kings.

sentences.t:
πὰρ γὰρ σοὶ πρώτῳ πασάμην Δημήτερος ἀκτὴν
ἤματι τῷ ὅτε μ’ εἷλες ἐϋκτιμένῃ ἐν ἀλωῇ,
καί μ’ ἐπέρασσας ἄνευθεν ἄγων πατρός τε φίλων τε
Λῆμνον ἐς ἠγαθέην, ἑκατόμβοιον δέ τοι ἦλφον.
sentences.tr:
par gar soi prōtōi pasamēn Dēmēteros aktēn
ēmati tōi hote m’ heiles eÿktimenēi en alōēi,
kai m’ eperassas aneuthen agōn patros te philōn te
Lēmnon es ēgatheēn, hekatomboion de toi ēlphon.
sentences.l:
For beside you first I tasted the meal of Demeter
on the day when you took me in the well-built orchard,
and sold me, leading me away from my father and my dear ones,
to holy Lemnos, and worth a hundred oxen I brought you in;
sentences.i: For it was at your side that I first ate the meal of Demeter, on the day you took me in the well-tilled orchard and sold me, leading me away from my father and my dear ones, to holy Lemnos; and I brought you in the worth of a hundred oxen.
sentences.n: Lycaon’s first argument is that he has already been Achilles’ captive and eaten his bread. πασάμην is an aorist of πατέομαι ‘taste, eat’, and Δημήτερος ἀκτήν ‘the meal of Demeter’ is ordinary bread, the food of mortals. πὰρ … σοὶ πρώτῳ ‘beside you first’ gives the place and time. εἷλες is an aorist of αἱρέω ‘seize, take’. ἐϋκτιμένῃ ἐν ἀλωῇ is the orchard of line 36 again; ἐϋκτιμένη is more usual of houses and towns. ἐπέρασσας ‘you sold’ repeats ἐπέρασσε (40), and ἄνευθεν ‘far from’ takes the genitive. ἑκατόμβοιον ‘worth a hundred oxen’ and ἦλφον, an aorist of ἀλφάνω ‘bring in, earn’, say what he was worth. τοι is again τοι = σοι.

sentences.t: νῦν δὲ λύμην τρὶς τόσσα πορών·
sentences.tr: nyn de lymēn tris tossa porōn·
sentences.l: And now I was ransomed, having given thrice as much;
sentences.i: And now I have been ransomed, paying thrice as much;
sentences.n: λύμην is a first-person aorist middle of λύω, an old short form without the -σα- (as in ἐλυσάμην), read here as ‘I got myself ransomed’. πορών is the aorist participle of a verb ‘give, furnish’ (aorist ἔπορον). τρὶς τόσσα is ‘thrice as much’, meaning three times the price Jason’s son had paid (41). Line 42 says it was Eetion who paid; Lycaon speaks as if the payment were his. The unit ends in the middle of line 80.

sentences.t:
ἠὼς δέ μοί ἐστιν
ἥδε δυωδεκάτη, ὅτ’ ἐς Ἴλιον εἰλήλουθα
πολλὰ παθών·
sentences.tr:
ēōs de moi estin
hēde dyōdekatē, hot’ es Ilion eilēloutha
polla pathōn·
sentences.i: and this is the twelfth dawn for me since I came to Ilium, after suffering much;
sentences.n: The unit begins in the middle of line 80. ἠὼς … ἥδε δυωδεκάτη ‘this twelfth dawn’ counts the days as the narrator did at lines 45–46. εἰλήλουθα is a perfect of ἔρχομαι, and ἐς Ἴλιον ‘to Ilium’ is Troy. πολλὰ παθών is ‘having suffered much’, the aorist participle of πάσχω. The unit ends after the second word of line 82.

sentences.t:
νῦν αὖ με τεῇς ἐν χερσὶν ἔθηκε
μοῖρ’ ὀλοή·
sentences.tr:
nyn au me teēis en chersin ethēke
moir’ oloē·
sentences.l:
now again into your hands me has put
the deadly fate;
sentences.i: now once more the deadly fate has put me in your hands;
sentences.n: The unit begins in the middle of line 82. νῦν αὖ is ‘now again’, and τεῇς is the epic form of σῇς ‘your’. ἔθηκε is an aorist of τίθημι ‘put, placed’, and its subject is the last words, μοῖρ’ ὀλοή, ‘the deadly fate’. μοῖρα is a person’s portion and fate, and ὀλοή is ‘deadly’. The unit ends at the ano teleia in line 83.

sentences.t:
μέλλω που ἀπεχθέσθαι Διὶ πατρί,
ὅς με σοὶ αὖτις δῶκε·
sentences.tr:
mellō pou apechthesthai Dii patri,
hos me soi autis dōke·
sentences.l:
I am destined, I suppose, to become hateful to father Zeus,
who gave me to you again;
sentences.i: I must be hateful to father Zeus, I suppose, who has given me over to you again;
sentences.n: The unit begins after the ano teleia in line 83. μέλλω with the infinitive is ‘I am destined to’, που is ‘I suppose’, and ἀπεχθέσθαι, an aorist infinitive of ἀπέχθομαι, is ‘to become hateful’. Διὶ πατρί is the dative ‘to father Zeus’. ὅς … δῶκε ‘who gave’ puts the blame on Zeus for returning him to Achilles. The unit ends in the middle of line 84.

sentences.t:
μινυνθάδιον δέ με μήτηρ
γείνατο Λαοθόη θυγάτηρ Ἄλταο γέροντος
Ἄλτεω, ὃς Λελέγεσσι φιλοπτολέμοισιν ἀνάσσει
Πήδασον αἰπήεσσαν ἔχων ἐπὶ Σατνιόεντι.
sentences.tr:
minynthadion de me mētēr
geinato Laothoē thygatēr Altao gerontos
Alteō, hos Lelegessi philoptolemoisin anassei
Pēdason aipēessan echōn epi Satnioenti.
sentences.l:
and short-lived me my mother
bore, Laothoe, daughter of old Altes,
Altes, who over the war-loving Leleges is lord
holding steep Pedasus on the Satnioeis.
sentences.i: and my mother bore me short-lived, Laothoe, the daughter of old Altes, Altes, who is lord over the war-loving Leleges and holds steep Pedasus on the Satnioeis.
sentences.n: The unit begins in the middle of line 84. μινυνθάδιον ‘short-lived’ is a predicate: ‘bore me short-lived’. The line sets out his birth: Λαοθόη is his mother, and the genitives Ἄλταο and Ἄλτεω are the two forms of the genitive of Ἄλτης, the name repeated. Λελέγεσσι is a dative plural in -εσσι, the Leleges being a people on the Trojan side, and ἀνάσσει takes the dative, ‘is lord over’. Πήδασον αἰπήεσσαν ‘steep Pedasus’ is a town, ἔχων ‘holding’ means he owns it, and ἐπὶ Σατνιόεντι ‘on the Satnioeis’ is the river on which it stands.

sentences.t: τοῦ δ’ ἔχε θυγατέρα Πρίαμος, πολλὰς δὲ καὶ ἄλλας·
sentences.tr: tou d’ eche thygatera Priamos, pollas de kai allas·
sentences.l: His daughter Priam had, and many, too, others;
sentences.i: Priam had his daughter to wife, and many other women besides;
sentences.n: τοῦ ‘his’ is Altes’, and ἔχε, ‘had’, means ‘had to wife’. πολλὰς δὲ καὶ ἄλλας ‘and many others too’ are Priam’s other wives, and the word for ‘wives’ is left to be understood. Lycaon is telling Achilles that Priam had many wives, which prepares the point that he is not Hector’s full brother (see 95). Line 88 is metrically irregular as transmitted: the first syllable of θυγατέρα, short by nature, is lengthened to serve as the long of the second foot, and καί is shortened before ἄλλας.

sentences.t:
τῆς δὲ δύω γενόμεσθα, σὺ δ’ ἄμφω δειροτομήσεις,
ἤτοι τὸν πρώτοισι μετὰ πρυλέεσσι δάμασσας
ἀντίθεον Πολύδωρον, ἐπεὶ βάλες ὀξέϊ δουρί·
sentences.tr:
tēs de dyō genomestha, sy d’ amphō deirotomēseis,
ētoi ton prōtoisi meta pryleessi damassas
antitheon Polydōron, epei bales oxeï douri·
sentences.i: She bore two of us, and you will cut the throats of both: the one, godlike Polydorus, you overcame among the foremost foot-soldiers, when you struck him with a sharp spear;
sentences.n: τῆς ‘of her’ is Laothoe, and γενόμεσθα is the epic form of ἐγενόμεθα ‘we were born’, without the augment. δειροτομήσεις is a future, ‘you will cut the throat of’ the two; since Polydorus fell to a spear (91), the verb is used loosely for ‘kill’, and his death is already past in δάμασσας, ‘you overcame’. ἤτοι is one word in this edition and marks the first of the two, τὸν ‘that one’. πρώτοισι μετὰ πρυλέεσσι is ‘among the foremost foot-soldiers’, and ἀντίθεον ‘godlike’ is the epithet of Polydorus. βάλες is ἔβαλες without the augment, and ὀξέϊ δουρί ‘with a sharp spear’.

sentences.t: νῦν δὲ δὴ ἐνθάδ’ ἐμοὶ κακὸν ἔσσεται·
sentences.tr: nyn de dē enthad’ emoi kakon essetai·
sentences.l: And now here for me evil will be;
sentences.i: And now evil is in store for me here;
sentences.n: νῦν δὲ δή ‘and now indeed’ turns from the past to the present; ἐνθάδ’ ‘here’ and κακὸν ἔσσεται ‘evil will be’, with ἔσσεται an epic form of ἔσται. The unit ends in the middle of line 92, at the ano teleia.

sentences.t:
οὐ γὰρ ὀΐω
σὰς χεῖρας φεύξεσθαι, ἐπεί ῥ’ ἐπέλασσέ γε δαίμων.
sentences.tr:
ou gar oïō
sas cheiras pheuxesthai, epei rh’ epelasse ge daimōn.
sentences.l:
for I do not think
that I shall escape your hands, since a power has brought me near.
sentences.i: for I do not think I shall escape your hands, since some power has brought me near.
sentences.n: The unit begins in the middle of line 92. ὀΐω ‘I think’ is an epic form of οἴομαι, and φεύξεσθαι is a future infinitive, ‘that I shall escape’. ἐπέλασσε, the aorist of πελάζω ‘bring near’, has no object in the Greek; ‘me’ is understood. δαίμων is a ‘power’, an unnamed divine force, the same word that stood in δαίμονι ἶσος at line 18.

sentences.t: ἄλλο δέ τοι ἐρέω, σὺ δ’ ἐνὶ φρεσὶ βάλλεο σῇσι·
sentences.tr: allo de toi ereō, sy d’ eni phresi balleo sēisi·
sentences.l: And another thing to you I will say, and you in your own mind lay it:
sentences.i: And I will tell you something else; lay it up in your own mind:
sentences.n: The line stands word for word at 1.297, where Achilles says it to Agamemnon, and the English is the same. τοι is σοι ‘to you’, and ἐρέω is a future ‘I will say’. βάλλεο is a middle imperative in the uncontracted epic form, ‘put, lay’, and σῇσι is an epic dative plural of σός ‘your own’. ἐνὶ φρεσὶ βάλλεο ‘lay it in your mind’ asks Achilles to take what follows to heart.

sentences.t:
μή με κτεῖν’, ἐπεὶ οὐχ ὁμογάστριος Ἕκτορός εἰμι,
ὅς τοι ἑταῖρον ἔπεφνεν ἐνηέα τε κρατερόν τε.
sentences.tr:
mē me ktein’, epei ouch homogastrios Hektoros eimi,
hos toi hetairon epephnen enēea te krateron te.
sentences.l:
Do not kill me, since I am not of the same womb as Hector,
who killed your companion, kindly and strong.”
sentences.i: Do not kill me, since I am not from the same womb as Hector, who killed your companion, kindly and strong.”
sentences.n: Here is the point of the plea. κτεῖν’ is κτεῖνε, a present imperative with μή, ‘do not kill me’. ὁμογάστριος ‘of the same belly’ is a full brother, with the same mother; Lycaon and Hector share a father but not a mother. ὅς is Hector, and ἑταῖρον ‘companion’ is Patroclus, left unnamed. ἐνηέα ‘kindly’ and κρατερόν ‘strong’ are accusatives agreeing with ἑταῖρον, joined by τε … τε. Achilles answers in the next part.
